citations.title: A Social Learning Theory Analysis of Peer-to-Peer Problem Solving and Shadow IT Emergence: A Case Study Approach
contexts: The results of this study reinforce the value of applying Social Learning Theory [5] to understand the spread of Shadow IT in digital organizations.

This study uses an exploratory qualitative design to understand how peer-to-peer (P2P) problem solving in a digital workplace can trigger Shadow IT, interpreted through Social Learning Theory (SLT) [5], [14].
This study draws on a conceptual model that blends Social Learning Theory [5], [14] with the realities of Shadow IT adoption in digital work environments.
Items mapped to SLT’s mechanisms [5] and drew on established constructs for perceived usefulness and diffusion to validate the qualitative patterns around adoption drivers.
SLT provides the lens for identifying three learning mechanisms: observational learning, modeling, and social reinforcement [5], [14].
These findings confirm that social learning mechanisms in the workplace occur through observational learning, modeling, and social reinforcement [5].

The spread of Shadow IT in the case study organization can be explained through three interconnected mechanisms from Social Learning Theory [5]: observational learning, modeling, and social reinforcement (Table V).
To make sense of this phenomenon, Social Learning Theory [5] offers a useful lens.

…and simple agreement patterns) were used to cross-check the qualitative interpretation: items targeting observational learning, modeling, and social reinforcement [5] were examined alongside usefulness and recommendation intent grounded in technology-adoption and diffusion logic [15], [16].

…and observation data abductively against SLT’s three elements: (i) observational learning (what people saw working for colleagues), (ii) modeling (how those behaviors were copied and routinized), and (iii) social reinforcement (how encouragement and visible efficiency gains sustained use) [5].

citations.title: Can Ethical Political Leadership Restore Public Trust in Political Leaders?
contexts: Theoretically, this article supports social exchange (Bandura, 1977, 1986) and social learning (Blau, 1964) theory, which explains how ethical political leadership practices can positively affect public trust in political leaders.

SLT can be broadly understood as a social behavioural approach that underlines the reciprocal interaction between cognitive, behavioral and environmental determinants of human behaviour and actions (Bandura, 1977).

Drawing on social learning theory (Bandura, 1977, 1986) and social exchange theory (Blau, 1964), the study maintains that the party political leadership process cascades or trickles down from party leaders to local leaders and then to the community.
